title: Software Design: OOP, SOLID, Design Patterns & Microservice Patterns
full_title: Software Design: OOP, SOLID, Design Patterns & Microservice Patterns: L2 → L3 Interview Preparation
level: OOP principles → SOLID → classic patterns in Python → distributed/microservice patterns → design review scenarios

sections.title: Mental model: why design principles exist
sections.intro_md:
**All of these principles answer one question: when requirements change, how much code do I have to touch, and how much can break?**

```
           HIGH COUPLING (bad)                          LOW COUPLING, HIGH COHESION (good)
 ┌──────────┐   knows internals of   ┌──────────┐       ┌──────────┐  depends on   ┌───────────┐
 │ Agent    │──────────────────────► │ Bedrock  │       │ Agent    │─────────────► │ LLMClient │ (interface)
 │ service  │  boto3 calls, retry    │ SDK code │       │ service  │               └─────▲─────┘
 └──────────┘  logic, JSON parsing   └──────────┘       └──────────┘          ┌──────────┴─────────┐
 change provider → rewrite agent service                                 BedrockClient    FakeClient (tests)
                                                        change provider → add one class; agent untouched
```
- **Coupling** = how much one module depends on another's details. Lower is better.
- **Cohesion** = how focused one module is on one job. Higher is better.
- Patterns are **named, proven shapes** for common problems — vocabulary for design discussions, not goals in themselves.

questions.title: The four pillars of OOP
questions.short_md: class Account: def __init__(self): self._balance = 0            # "private" by convention def deposit(self, amount: int) -> None: if amount <= 0: raise ValueError("amount must be positive")   # invariant protected self._balance += amount @property def balance(self) -> int: return self._balance        # read-only view

questions.title: Composition over inheritance
questions.short_md: Prefer building objects **from** other objects ("has-a") over deep class hierarchies ("is-a"). Inheritance couples the child to the parent's internals; composition lets you swap parts.

questions.title: DRY, KISS, YAGNI
questions.short_md: - **DRY** (Don't Repeat Yourself): one source of truth for each piece of *knowledge* (not every similar-looking line). Duplicating code twice is fine; abstract on the third time when the shape is clear. - **KISS** (Keep It Simple): the simplest design that meets requirements. - **YAGNI** (You Aren't Gonna Need It): don't build for imagined future needs.
questions.body_md:
- **DRY** (Don't Repeat Yourself): one source of truth for each piece of *knowledge* (not every similar-looking line). Duplicating code twice is fine; abstract on the third time when the shape is clear.
- **KISS** (Keep It Simple): the simplest design that meets requirements.
- **YAGNI** (You Aren't Gonna Need It): don't build for imagined future needs.

**Pitfall:** wrong abstraction is worse than duplication — merging two things that only *look* alike creates coupling that breaks when they diverge.

questions.title: Interfaces in Python: ABC vs Protocol
questions.short_md: Python has no `interface` keyword. **ABC** = nominal (classes must inherit and implement abstract methods; error at instantiation). **Protocol** = structural (any class with matching methods fits; checked by mypy/pyright). Use Protocols for ports like `LLMClient` so third-party classes fit without inheriting. Details in 01 Q20.

sections.title: SOLID
sections.intro_md: **SOLID = five principles for classes/modules that are easy to change.** Examples use one domain: a document-processing service.

questions.title: S — Single Responsibility Principle
questions.short_md: A class should have **one reason to change** — one owner/stakeholder.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** A class should have **one reason to change** — one owner/stakeholder.

```python
# ❌ one class changes when the parsing rules, the storage, OR the email template changes
class InvoiceProcessor:
    def parse(self, pdf): ...
    def save_to_s3(self, data): ...
    def email_finance(self, data): ...

# ✅ separate reasons to change; a small coordinator wires them
class InvoiceParser:    def parse(self, pdf) -> Invoice: ...
class InvoiceRepository: def save(self, inv: Invoice) -> None: ...
class FinanceNotifier:  def notify(self, inv: Invoice) -> None: ...

class ProcessInvoice:                      # use case / service
    def __init__(self, parser, repo, notifier): ...
    def __call__(self, pdf):
        inv = self.parser.parse(pdf); self.repo.save(inv); self.notifier.notify(inv)
```

questions.title: O — Open/Closed Principle
questions.short_md: Open for **extension**, closed for **modification** — add new behaviour by adding code, not by editing a growing `if/elif` chain.

questions.title: L — Liskov Substitution Principle
questions.short_md: A subclass must be usable anywhere its parent is expected **without surprising the caller** — same contract: accepts at least the same inputs, returns the same kind of output, doesn't throw new unexpected errors.

questions.title: I — Interface Segregation Principle
questions.short_md: Clients shouldn't depend on methods they don't use. Prefer several small interfaces over one fat one.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** Clients shouldn't depend on methods they don't use. Prefer several small interfaces over one fat one.

```python
from typing import Protocol
class DocReader(Protocol):
    def get(self, doc_id: str) -> bytes: ...
class DocWriter(Protocol):
    def put(self, doc_id: str, data: bytes) -> None: ...

def summarise(reader: DocReader, doc_id: str): ...   # needs only read → easy to fake, least privilege
```
The same idea applies to agent tools: give an agent a narrow `read_ticket` tool, not a `jira_admin` tool with 40 operations.

questions.title: D — Dependency Inversion Principle
questions.short_md: High-level business logic should depend on **abstractions**, not on concrete infrastructure. Infrastructure implements the abstraction. Combined with **dependency injection** (pass dependencies in, don't create them inside), this makes code testable and swappable.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** High-level business logic should depend on **abstractions**, not on concrete infrastructure. Infrastructure implements the abstraction. Combined with **dependency injection** (pass dependencies in, don't create them inside), this makes code testable and swappable.

```python
class LLMClient(Protocol):
    def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str: ...

class TicketTriage:                                 # business logic: knows nothing about Bedrock
    def __init__(self, llm: LLMClient):
        self.llm = llm
    def triage(self, text: str) -> str:
        return self.llm.complete(f"Classify: {text}")

# production
triage = TicketTriage(BedrockLLM(model_id=...))
# test
class FakeLLM:
    def complete(self, prompt): return "billing"
assert TicketTriage(FakeLLM()).triage("charged twice") == "billing"
```
FastAPI's `Depends` (20 Q10) is DI at the framework level; "ports and adapters" / hexagonal architecture (01 Q48) is DIP at the architecture level.

sections.title: Classic design patterns in Python
sections.intro_md: **Three families (Gang of Four):** *Creational* (how objects are made), *Structural* (how objects are combined), *Behavioural* (how objects interact). In Python many patterns are simpler because functions are first-class objects.

questions.title: Singleton — and why it's usually a module
questions.short_md: Ensures one instance (e.g. one config, one connection pool). In Python a **module is already a singleton** (imported once), so a module-level object or `functools.cache` on a factory is the idiomatic version.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** Ensures one instance (e.g. one config, one connection pool). In Python a **module is already a singleton** (imported once), so a module-level object or `functools.cache` on a factory is the idiomatic version.

```python
# settings.py
from functools import cache
@cache
def get_settings() -> Settings:
    return Settings()          # created once, reused everywhere
```
**Pitfall:** singletons are global state — hard to test and unsafe to mutate across threads. Prefer creating once at startup (FastAPI lifespan) and injecting.

questions.title: Factory (and Abstract Factory)
questions.short_md: A function/class that decides **which concrete class to create**, so callers don't hard-code it.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** A function/class that decides **which concrete class to create**, so callers don't hard-code it.

```python
def make_llm(provider: str, **kw) -> LLMClient:
    match provider:
        case "bedrock": return BedrockLLM(**kw)
        case "openai":  return OpenAILLM(**kw)
        case "fake":    return FakeLLM()
        case _: raise ValueError(f"unknown provider {provider}")

llm = make_llm(settings.llm_provider, model_id=settings.model_id)
```
LangChain's `init_chat_model("provider:model")` is a factory. **Abstract factory** = a factory for a *family* of related objects (e.g. AWS vs local: storage + queue + secrets together).

questions.title: Builder
questions.short_md: Constructs a complex object step by step, often with a fluent API, separating construction from the final object. Python's keyword arguments and dataclasses remove most needs for it; it's still useful for complex, validated, multi-step construction.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** Constructs a complex object step by step, often with a fluent API, separating construction from the final object. Python's keyword arguments and dataclasses remove most needs for it; it's still useful for complex, validated, multi-step construction.

```python
graph = StateGraph(State)                 # LangGraph's StateGraph is a builder:
graph.add_node("plan", plan)
graph.add_edge(START, "plan")
app = graph.compile(checkpointer=saver)  # build() → immutable runnable object
```

questions.title: Strategy
questions.short_md: Define a family of interchangeable algorithms and choose one at runtime. In Python, a strategy is often just a function passed in.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** Define a family of interchangeable algorithms and choose one at runtime. In Python, a strategy is often just a function passed in.

```python
def fixed_chunks(text, size=1000): ...
def by_headings(text): ...
def semantic_chunks(text): ...

CHUNKERS = {"fixed": fixed_chunks, "headings": by_headings, "semantic": semantic_chunks}

def index_document(text, strategy="headings"):
    for chunk in CHUNKERS[strategy](text):
        embed_and_store(chunk)
```
Other examples: retry/backoff policies, pricing rules, model routing (cheap vs strong model).

questions.title: Observer / pub-sub
questions.short_md: Subjects notify subscribers when something happens, without knowing who they are. In-process it's callbacks/event hooks; across services it becomes pub/sub (SNS, EventBridge).

questions.title: Adapter and Facade
questions.short_md: - **Adapter:** converts one interface into the one your code expects. E.g. wrap a vendor SDK so it matches your `LLMClient` Protocol; MCP servers are adapters that turn APIs into a standard tool interface. - **Facade:** a simple front over a complicated subsystem. E.g. `DocumentService.ingest(file)` hides upload → Textract → chunk → embed → index.
questions.body_md:
- **Adapter:** converts one interface into the one your code expects. E.g. wrap a vendor SDK so it matches your `LLMClient` Protocol; MCP servers are adapters that turn APIs into a standard tool interface.
- **Facade:** a simple front over a complicated subsystem. E.g. `DocumentService.ingest(file)` hides upload → Textract → chunk → embed → index.

questions.title: Decorator pattern (vs Python `@decorator`)
questions.short_md: The pattern wraps an object to add behaviour while keeping the same interface (the `RetryingClient` in Q02). Python's `@decorator` syntax applies the same idea to **functions** — logging, retries, caching, auth checks.

questions.title: Repository and Unit of Work
questions.short_md: **Repository** = a collection-like interface for loading/saving domain objects, hiding the database. **Unit of Work** = groups changes into one transaction and commits/rolls back together.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** **Repository** = a collection-like interface for loading/saving domain objects, hiding the database. **Unit of Work** = groups changes into one transaction and commits/rolls back together.

```python
class DocumentRepo(Protocol):
    def get(self, doc_id: str) -> Document | None: ...
    def add(self, doc: Document) -> None: ...

class SqlDocumentRepo:
    def __init__(self, session): self.session = session
    def get(self, doc_id): return self.session.get(DocumentRow, doc_id)
    def add(self, doc): self.session.add(doc)

async with uow:                      # Unit of Work wraps the session/transaction
    doc = uow.documents.get(doc_id)
    doc.mark_processed()
    await uow.commit()
```
Business logic gets tested with an in-memory repo; SQLAlchemy's `Session` is itself a unit of work.

questions.title: Command and Chain of Responsibility
questions.short_md: - **Command:** turn a request into an object (`{"action": "refund", "order": "A12", "amount": 50}`) that can be queued, logged, retried, approved or undone. Agent **tool calls** are commands — which is why you can validate and require approval before executing them. - **Chain of Responsibility:** pass a request along a chain of handlers, each may handle/modify/stop it. **Middleware** in FastAPI and LangChain v1 agents is this pattern (auth → rate limit → logging → handler).

- **Command:** turn a request into an object (`{"action": "refund", "order": "A12", "amount": 50}`) that can be queued, logged, retried, approved or undone. Agent **tool calls** are commands — which is why you can validate and require approval before executing them.
- **Chain of Responsibility:** pass a request along a chain of handlers, each may handle/modify/stop it. **Middleware** in FastAPI and LangChain v1 agents is this pattern (auth → rate limit → logging → handler).

questions.title: Template Method
questions.short_md: A base class defines the fixed steps of an algorithm; subclasses fill in specific steps.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** A base class defines the fixed steps of an algorithm; subclasses fill in specific steps.

```python
class Ingestor(ABC):
    def run(self, src):                 # fixed skeleton
        raw = self.fetch(src)
        text = self.extract(raw)        # varies per source
        return self.index(self.chunk(text))
    @abstractmethod
    def extract(self, raw): ...
```
Python alternative: pass the varying step as a function (strategy) — often simpler.

questions.title: Monolith vs modular monolith vs microservices
questions.short_md: **L3 answer:** "Start modular; split a service out when there's a concrete reason — different scaling profile (GPU/agent workers vs API), different release cadence, separate team ownership, or a fault-isolation/security boundary." Microservices are an organisational scaling tool, not a default.
questions.body_md:
| | Monolith | Modular monolith | Microservices |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deploy | one unit | one unit, strong internal module boundaries | many independent units |
| Pros | simple dev, testing, transactions | simple + clean boundaries; easy to split later | independent deploy/scale, team autonomy, fault isolation |
| Cons | tangles as it grows | discipline needed | network failures, distributed data, ops/observability cost |

**L3 answer:** "Start modular; split a service out when there's a concrete reason — different scaling profile (GPU/agent workers vs API), different release cadence, separate team ownership, or a fault-isolation/security boundary." Microservices are an organisational scaling tool, not a default.

questions.title: Domain-Driven Design basics: bounded contexts
questions.short_md: Split a system by **business capability**, where each area (bounded context) has its own model and language. "Document" means a file in *Ingestion*, a set of chunks in *Search*, and a billable unit in *Billing*. Service boundaries usually follow bounded contexts; each owns its data (**database per service** — other services use its API/events, not its tables).

questions.title: API Gateway and Backend-for-Frontend (BFF)
questions.short_md: - **API Gateway:** single entry point → routing, auth (JWT validation), rate limits, TLS, request validation. (AWS API Gateway, ALB + middleware.) - **BFF:** a backend tailored to one frontend (web vs mobile) that aggregates downstream calls and shapes responses, so the UI doesn't make 6 calls. A FastAPI layer between React and AgentCore is effectively a BFF.

questions.title: Resilience patterns: timeout, retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead
questions.short_md: cycle: Circuit breaker states CLOSED > Calls flow normally; failures are counted. OPEN > Too many failures → fail fast without calling the dependency; use a fallback. HALF-OPEN > After a cool-down, let a few trial calls through. exit > Trial calls succeed → back to CLOSED. They fail → OPEN again.
questions.body_md:
```flow
cycle: Circuit breaker states
CLOSED > Calls flow normally; failures are counted.
OPEN > Too many failures → fail fast without calling the dependency; use a fallback.
HALF-OPEN > After a cool-down, let a few trial calls through.
exit > Trial calls succeed → back to CLOSED. They fail → OPEN again.
```

```
            timeout              retry (backoff + jitter)       circuit breaker
 caller ──► every call has  ──►  only for transient,       ──►  CLOSED: calls flow
            a deadline           idempotent operations          too many failures → OPEN: fail fast
                                 with a retry budget            after cool-down → HALF-OPEN: try a few
 bulkhead: separate pools/queues/concurrency limits per dependency, so one slow dependency can't use every worker
```

```python
class CircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, threshold=5, cooldown=30):
        self.fails, self.threshold, self.cooldown, self.opened_at = 0, threshold, cooldown, None
    def call(self, fn, *a, **kw):
        if self.opened_at and time.monotonic() - self.opened_at < self.cooldown:
            raise CircuitOpenError("dependency unavailable")       # fail fast, use fallback
        try:
            result = fn(*a, **kw)
        except Exception:
            self.fails += 1
            if self.fails >= self.threshold:
                self.opened_at = time.monotonic()
            raise
        self.fails, self.opened_at = 0, None                       # success → close
        return result
```
**Why it matters for LLM apps:** when a model provider is degraded, a breaker switches to a fallback model or a "try later" message instead of piling up slow requests (18 Q25).

questions.title: Saga pattern (distributed transactions)
questions.short_md: A business transaction across services is split into **local transactions**, each with a **compensating action** that undoes it if a later step fails. No global lock or two-phase commit.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** A business transaction across services is split into **local transactions**, each with a **compensating action** that undoes it if a later step fails. No global lock or two-phase commit.

```flow
sequence: Saga: booking a trip
actors: Saga, Flights, Hotels, Payments
Saga -> Flights: reserve flight
Saga -> Hotels: reserve hotel
Saga -> Payments: charge card
Payments --> Saga: ✗ fails
> No global transaction exists, so undo the earlier steps in reverse order.
Saga -> Hotels: cancel hotel (compensation)
Saga -> Flights: cancel flight (compensation)
```
| Style | How | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **Orchestration** | a coordinator (Step Functions, LangGraph) calls each step and its compensation | clear flow, central visibility; coordinator is a dependency |
| **Choreography** | each service reacts to events and emits the next | loose coupling; flow is hard to see/debug |

Compensations must be idempotent and may not perfectly undo (an email can't be unsent → design "send" as the last step). Step Functions implementation: 15 Q13.

questions.title: Transactional outbox
questions.short_md: Solves "I updated my DB and need to publish an event, but either could fail" (dual-write problem). Write the event into an **outbox table in the same DB transaction** as the business change; a separate relay publishes outbox rows to the queue and marks them sent.

questions.title: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)
questions.short_md: Use **different models for writes (commands) and reads (queries)**. The write side keeps normalised, validated data; one or more read models are denormalised for fast queries and updated from events.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** Use **different models for writes (commands) and reads (queries)**. The write side keeps normalised, validated data; one or more read models are denormalised for fast queries and updated from events.

```flow
sequence: CQRS: separate write and read models
actors: Client, Write model, Projector, Read model
Client -> Write model: POST /orders
> Validated and stored in the normalised write store (e.g. Postgres).
Write model -> Projector: event: order.created
Projector -> Read model: update denormalised view
> E.g. DynamoDB, OpenSearch or a cache, shaped for fast queries.
Client -> Read model: GET /dashboard
Read model --> Client: fast read (eventually consistent)
```
Use when reads and writes have very different shapes/scale (dashboards, search). Cost: eventual consistency between sides and more moving parts — don't use it for simple CRUD.

questions.title: Event sourcing
questions.short_md: Store the **sequence of events** (`DocumentUploaded`, `ExtractionCompleted`, `ApprovedBy(u42)`) as the source of truth, and derive current state by replaying them. Gives a full audit trail and time travel.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** Store the **sequence of events** (`DocumentUploaded`, `ExtractionCompleted`, `ApprovedBy(u42)`) as the source of truth, and derive current state by replaying them. Gives a full audit trail and time travel.

Costs: event schema versioning, replay time (use snapshots), harder queries (usually paired with CQRS read models). LangGraph checkpoints are similar in spirit — a history of state snapshots you can replay or fork (07 Q14).

questions.title: Strangler fig, sidecar, anti-corruption layer
questions.short_md: - **Strangler fig:** migrate a legacy system piece by piece behind a router until the old one can be removed (18 Q27). - **Sidecar:** a helper container next to the app in the same task/pod (log router, proxy, OTel collector) — ECS sidecars (13 Q07). - **Anti-corruption layer:** an adapter between your clean model and a messy legacy/vendor model so its concepts don't leak into your code.
questions.body_md:
- **Strangler fig:** migrate a legacy system piece by piece behind a router until the old one can be removed (18 Q27).
- **Sidecar:** a helper container next to the app in the same task/pod (log router, proxy, OTel collector) — ECS sidecars (13 Q07).
- **Anti-corruption layer:** an adapter between your clean model and a messy legacy/vendor model so its concepts don't leak into your code.

questions.title: Sync vs async communication; idempotent consumers
questions.short_md: Synchronous (HTTP/gRPC) is simple but couples availability — if B is down, A fails. Asynchronous (queues/events) decouples and buffers spikes but adds eventual consistency and at-least-once delivery → every consumer must be **idempotent** (dedupe by message/operation ID). See 18 Q08–Q10.

questions.title: The Twelve-Factor App (headline list)
questions.short_md: Codebase in VCS · explicit dependencies · **config in environment** · backing services as attached resources · build/release/run separated · **stateless processes** · port binding · scale by processes · **disposability** (fast start, graceful SIGTERM) · dev/prod parity · logs as event streams · admin tasks as one-off processes. Containers on ECS follow these naturally (10 Q22).

questions.title: Refactor a 2,000-line `agent_service.py` that does everything
questions.short_md: 1. Add characterisation tests around current behaviour first. 2. Identify responsibilities: HTTP handling, auth, prompt building, LLM calls, tool execution, persistence, notifications. 3. Extract by responsibility (SRP) behind small interfaces (ISP/DIP): `LLMClient`, `ToolRegistry`, `JobRepository`, `Notifier`. 4. Replace `if tool == ...` chains with a registry (OCP). 5. Inject dependencies at startup; tests use fakes. 6. Do it incrementally, one extraction per PR, behaviour unchanged.
questions.body_md:
1. Add characterisation tests around current behaviour first.
2. Identify responsibilities: HTTP handling, auth, prompt building, LLM calls, tool execution, persistence, notifications.
3. Extract by responsibility (SRP) behind small interfaces (ISP/DIP): `LLMClient`, `ToolRegistry`, `JobRepository`, `Notifier`.
4. Replace `if tool == ...` chains with a registry (OCP).
5. Inject dependencies at startup; tests use fakes.
6. Do it incrementally, one extraction per PR, behaviour unchanged.

questions.title: "Should we split our FastAPI app into microservices?"
questions.short_md: Ask what problem it solves: Are parts scaling differently (CPU-heavy extraction vs I/O-heavy API)? Different teams blocked on one release train? Different security boundaries? If not, keep a modular monolith and fix module boundaries first. If yes, split the **one** part with the clearest boundary (e.g. document-extraction workers behind a queue), with its own data and contract tests.

questions.title: How do you avoid over-engineering in a design review?
questions.short_md: Tie every abstraction to a current requirement or a likely, cheap-to-support change; count the moving parts; prefer boring managed services; ask "what's the simplest version we could ship and measure?" Patterns are justified by the change they make easy — name that change.

sections.title: Cheat sheet
sections.intro_md:
| Concept | One-liner |
|---|---|
| Coupling / cohesion | depend on little; each module does one thing |
| Composition > inheritance | wrap and combine; inherit only for true is-a |
| SRP | one reason to change |
| OCP | extend by adding code (registry), not editing if/elif |
| LSP | subclasses keep the parent's contract |
| ISP | small, focused interfaces (and tools) |
| DIP + DI | logic depends on abstractions; inject implementations |
| Singleton | in Python: module object / cached factory; inject it |
| Factory | choose concrete class from config |
| Strategy | swap algorithms (often just functions) |
| Observer | publish events to subscribers |
| Adapter / Facade | convert interface / simplify subsystem |
| Repository / UoW | hide DB; one transaction per use case |
| Command / Chain | requests as objects (tool calls); middleware chains |
| Circuit breaker | fail fast when a dependency is down |
| Saga | local txns + compensations; orchestrated or choreographed |
| Outbox | event row in same txn → relay publishes |
| CQRS | separate write and read models |
| Event sourcing | events are the source of truth |
| Microservices | split for scaling/team/isolation reasons, not by default |
